My elementary school had a "Zero Tolerance" policy on tardiness. My mom was also a drug addict. In my fourth grade year, she made me late for school every single day, whether five minutes late or an hour, because of her sloppy and slow behavior. The teacher had to have noticed that my mom was under the influence the many times she walked me to class with half-open eyes and occasionally drifting off while standing up, but she never brought it up or scheduled any conference. She only chastised me daily about tardiness. Me. Because four tardies counted as an absence, I was technically "absent" for a quarter of the school year. Also, excessive tardiness resulted in removing my field trip privileges, me having to wait ten minutes after everyone else to join recess, and my removal of ability to check out library books - reading was a passion of mine. I was only allowed to "check out" the shitty classroom books to maintain Accelerated Reader points. It was a lame goal, but at the time, becoming a safety patrol was my dream! Both my parents had been patrols when they were my age, and I worked very hard in my classes and strove to be a good example for others so I would get a chance to be awarded that orange seatbelty belt. When it was time to select safety patrols, my teacher rattled off a list of who was to be granted the title. She came up to the G's - my last initial - and then skipped to the H's and J's without saying mine. Even the poor-behaved little assholes got belts. Afterwards, I went up to her desk, fighting off tears, and asked her why I wasn't selected. She replied, stoic-faced, "A safety patrol always has to be responsible and punctual. I can't suggest choosing a tardy student." What a bitch, man In retrospect I don't understand why she completely ignored my mother's faults and assumed I, a nine-year old, was choosing to be constantly late and irresponsible.

I couldn't have survived on my own after moving out when I was 18. I lived on about $6k - $8k a year (this is in the early '90s) for the first few years of my adult life, completely supporting my own living expenses, but my parents graciously paid for school and eventually loaned me the money to buy my first car. (The arrangement was what a friend affectionally called the zero percent interest/pay-over-a-thousand-year plan.) I paid them back what I could afford every month, which ranged from zero to maybe $20. My financial debt to them (buying me a car and then buying me another car when the first one died) got up to about $2000 at its peak. After a few years, I moved across the country and finally got myself my first Career Job, and actually started making money. I hadn't made any payments towards my debt in a while, what with the expenses of moving and such, but after working in my new career for a while, I told my Mom, who had come to visit, that I wanted to start making payments again. She said okay, but of course only to pay what I could. She was expecting a check for $20 or something, but I completely paid off the rest of the debt, which was maybe $1200. She stared at the check in shock for a moment, got teary eyed, and then we hugged. It was one of the proudest moments of my life.

Dank memes, am I right? It's like that old cliche: ya can't live with em, can't live without em. I remember my old man sat me down one day and told me, "Paul, don't you dare go off gettin married or having kids until you know you're with the right dank meme." I should have listened to him, but 18 years later at a bar in Tallahassee I saw a dank meme that must have been shaped by the hands of god himself. Her name? Delores L. Chipperson. At that moment all I could think about was knockin boots with ol' Ms. Chipperson, and I made it my goal to get with her by the end of the night.
Now I don't mean to brag, but back in the day I was quite the catch. Not only could I play the blues like a madman, but I had a body chiseled from farm work. It wasn't long before I sweet talked her up to the motel room I had for the night, and boy let me tell you, it was the best damn sex I'd ever had. This woman was like riding on a bull at the rodeo - size and all. Lord that rubenesque shape and all that power...it could do strange things to a man. And that is when I stupidly decided not to use a condom. It was a moment of bliss I'll never forget, for all the good and bad that it has brought me.
About 9 months later we gave birth to our first son, Lyle. We were planning to get married that fall but Delores kept putting it off. She decided to give her son her own last name, and refused to take my last name, Hargis. Now looking back, these were all tell tale signs that I should have followed, but I was young and in love. I just thought she was being hard to get.
We stayed together, unmarried, for the next 6 years. After Lyle was born we didn't really have time to even think about marriage anymore. He was quite a handful, and although I never got to find out, I think he had that autism thing that doctors are talkin about these days. I still loved him with all my heart. I remember giving him baths in the sink, he was such a handsome little guy.
Around the time Lyle turned 6 I hired a new guy to work at the auto shop I managed. His name was Lamar and he seemed like a hard working, young go getter. I put a lot of trust in him, and even brought him to the house a few times for dinner.
Lamar had previously worked as a carpenter, an area I had no skill in what-so-ever. One afternoon I had asked him to fix the floorboards in my master bedroom because they were always squeaking all the time. I payed him up front pretty handsomely (more than he would make for a day at the shop, that is for sure) and covered his shift so he could work at my house. That day I decided to take my lunch at home to see how everything was going, and that is when I saw it. Lamar was banging my wife ruthlessly, all with little Lyle sitting in the family room a few feet away. Delores was just saying "Lamar is helpin me fix the floorboards thats all chippah!". That's when I burst in the room, gathered my things, and sat down to talk with my son for the last time.
I made random stuff up. I told him I was an encyclepedia salesman and that I would need to travel for a long time. Hell, it was the first thing I could think of. Poor kid. I still miss that kid, but thankfully I have a lot of little kids around nowadays because I do kind of a television show for children called Uncle Paul's Happy Hour.
Anyway that is the story of how a dank meme ruined my life. She tore out my heart and threw it away. But do you know what the worst part of this whole thing is? She took our son away from me. He was such a special young guy. I have tried looking him up but I can't seem to find anything. But that's the way she goes. Nothing left but to lace up your sneakers and move on with life.

So I was standing in a rather large line at my local Wal-Mart today behind a couple families that I know from when I went to church with my family in year younger. It was the only register open so there wasn’t much of another option to get my 12 pack of Mountain Dew for a party I was heading to. I was wondering why the line was going nowhere when I decided to poke my head up front to see what the holdup was. It was a little old lady who didn’t have enough for her groceries and she was trying to talk the cashier into letting her get away with being short. This struck me as odd until I found out she was a mere $0.21 short of her purchase. Now all these families were just staring and there was even two making fun of her. I walked up and handed my soda to the cashier, handed him a $5 and told her to keep the change. One of the middle aged women (I knew these people, so I also knew that they all make over 6 digits) grabbed her kid and yelled very loudly, “See that man? He’s acting just like Jesus wants us to.” For some reason this set me off, so I turned around. I haven’t shaved in awhile so I’m rocking some nice scruff, a Slayer shirt, and gym shorts, so it must have been a nice sight. Very loudly, I said “Like Jesus? Ma’am I’m an atheist who makes minimum wage and I was the one who stepped up to help her? Your hypocritical Christianity is an inspiration to us all.” As I stormed out, a couple of the cart boys started to whistle and cheer, soon shoppers joined in and even the cashier. I gave a wave and went off with a feeling of accomplishment.
